Sentences: [00:00 - 00:03] Speaker 1: Ongoing dialogue with member schools and student athletes.
[00:04 - 00:12] Speaker 1: The NCAA Committee on Competitive Safeguards and Medical Aspect of Sport has developed guidance on the responsible use of performance technologies.
[00:13 - 00:26] Speaker 1: These recommendations focus on five key policy, education, data management, thoughtful adoption of new tools, and continuous improvement.
[00:26 - 00:34] Speaker 1: At their core, they aim to help schools harness innovation while safeguarding student athlete health, safety and performance.
[00:35 - 00:50] Speaker 1: Today's discussion will explore why this topic is so important right now, how these technologies are shaping the student athlete experience, and what it means to take a values driven, responsible approach moving forward.
[00:50 - 00:56] Speaker 1: I'm excited to welcome our panelists for today's conversation, Tim Coffey and Mark Koberly.
[00:57 - 01:06] Speaker 1: They both played a direct role in developing the performance technologies recommendations and I am so grateful to have them here with us to hear their insights.
[01:06 - 01:15] Speaker 1: Let's start off by having you both introduce yourselves and tell us a little bit about your experience with performance technologies in collegiate athletics.
[01:15 - 01:17] Speaker 1: Tim, let's go ahead and start with you.
[01:18 - 01:19] Speaker 2: Thanks Dina.
[01:19 - 01:19] Speaker 2: Thank you.
[01:19 - 01:27] Speaker 2: So, Tim Crockey I'm an Associate professor of kinesiology at Longwood University and I serve as our faculty athletics rep.
[01:27 - 01:39] Speaker 2: I'm a biomechanist by training, so most of my research has used some sort of performance tech, but more from a research standpoint looking at how injuries happen and what we can do to prevent them.
[01:39 - 01:42] Speaker 2: So that's kind of my experience with the technology itself.
[01:45 - 01:46] Speaker 3: I'm Mark Koberly.
[01:46 - 01:52] Speaker 3: I'm a Senior Associate Athletic Director for Sports Medicine, Welfare and Performance at Iowa State University.
[01:53 - 02:08] Speaker 3: Been in the sports medicine field by trade, an athletic trainer a long time and oversee and coordinate and ensure collaboration across all of our performance departments from sports medicine to mental health to nutrition to strength conditioning, sports science.
[02:10 - 02:18] Speaker 3: I was on the task force as a representative from the NATA and served as co chair of the Data analytics task force of the nat.
[02:20 - 02:20] Speaker 1: Great.
[02:20 - 02:23] Speaker 1: Thank you both again so much for being here.
[02:23 - 02:34] Speaker 1: It was so wonderful having you both part of this process of putting together these recommendations and having you give your time today to help us talk about this great work is is much appreciated.
[02:34 - 02:35] Speaker 1: So thank you again.
[02:36 - 02:45] Speaker 1: So Tim, why is responsible use of performance technology in collegiate athletics so pertinent today?
[02:47 - 02:49] Speaker 2: So for me this got started.
[02:49 - 03:04] Speaker 2: I was working with a student, we were doing a research project looking at ACL injury risk with basketball players and we had two student athletes who opted out of the research study which was perfectly fine.
[03:04 - 03:09] Speaker 2: But I wanted to follow up with them to really understand kind of why is that.
[03:09 - 03:11] Speaker 2: We were giving them information.
[03:11 - 03:16] Speaker 2: We were looking at how these injuries happen and we're trying to give them information on how to prevent it.
[03:17 - 03:24] Speaker 2: And so my follow up conversation with the student athletes is their focus was really about, I want to be an athlete, I want to be a student.
[03:24 - 03:28] Speaker 2: I don't want the number in my head that I could be at risk.
[03:29 - 03:43] Speaker 2: And so it made me kind of stop from a researcher standpoint and think about what is all this data that we're collecting and what are the impacts that it has on student athletes, as well as how accurate is some of the data that we're collecting.
[03:43 - 03:54] Speaker 2: The technology has advanced so fast that I think about when I first started collecting data and how long it took to digitize and collect a joint angle.
[03:54 - 04:00] Speaker 2: And now I can pull out my smartphone and I can do it in about 10 seconds.
[04:00 - 04:04] Speaker 2: And I was like, well, that would have solved me a month of work 20 years ago.
[04:06 - 04:14] Speaker 2: And so how accurate are some of the things that we have and how does that play into what we were then doing with our student athletes on the back end of that?
[04:17 - 04:18] Speaker 1: Yeah, those are some great points.
[04:18 - 04:48] Speaker 1: And I think back to the conversations that we had during the Performance Technology Summit and how we spoke about issues that student athletes would bring up even, even around who is even accessing this data that we're collecting and where is it being stored and how are folks applying this information to my playing time or my clearance to play.
[04:48 - 04:57] Speaker 1: And it just makes me think back on how student athletes were speaking up about what their experiences were in this particular area.
[04:58 - 05:07] Speaker 1: And Tim, when I think back too to your talk at the Performance Technology Summit, can you talk to us a little bit about the different types of tools?
[05:07 - 05:11] Speaker 1: There are so many different types of performance technologies out there.
[05:11 - 05:16] Speaker 1: Can you talk to us just a little bit about what some of those main categories might look like?
[05:17 - 05:17] Speaker 1: Sure.
[05:18 - 05:22] Speaker 2: So I think we oftentimes think of this performance tech as wearable technology.
[05:22 - 05:26] Speaker 2: The idea of fitness trackers with first kind of jumping in.
[05:26 - 05:38] Speaker 2: And so we've got wearable tech that goes on a student athlete that they wear in some form or capacity, whether that can be a sweat lactate patch that's put on them or a heart rate monitor.
[05:38 - 05:41] Speaker 2: But there's also devices that go on equipment.
[05:41 - 05:41] Speaker 2: Right.
[05:41 - 05:46] Speaker 2: We can put tags on bats and look at how swing speed is.
[05:46 - 05:48] Speaker 2: So we have equipment based pieces.
[05:49 - 06:14] Speaker 2: One of the fastest growing areas that we've seen are some of the optical or camera based systems that not only can track where position an athlete is on the field, but can utilize that technology to look at accelerations and velocities and all sorts of other metrics in regards to Performance, we've seen an increase in lab grade equipment because individuals have greater access to it.
[06:14 - 06:28] Speaker 2: So whether those are DEXA scanners or we're talking about in bodies, to look at body composition that are typically used within a lab setting, we see that those are getting used more with student athletes.
[06:29 - 06:32] Speaker 2: Force plates and force decks fall into that category as well.
[06:33 - 06:44] Speaker 2: And then the one area that gets kind of looked over oftentimes are a lot of surveys or self reports, web based or tablet based that student athletes fill out.
[06:44 - 07:06] Speaker 2: So those can be mood pieces, they can be sleep counters, it can be menstrual trackers, but it tends to be really personal information that gets tracked through some sort of survey and then integrated in within a student athlete management kind of network that then gets looked at with the other data that's collected.
[07:07 - 07:14] Speaker 1: Yeah, I bet it's really easy for people to overlook the surveys and not think of them as performance technology in the sense.
[07:14 - 07:19] Speaker 1: But we are collecting data and using that data to integrate it with other things.
[07:19 - 07:20] Speaker 1: So that makes sense.
[07:20 - 07:27] Speaker 1: How have you seen use cases evolve over the time that you've been looking into the research behind performance technologies?
[07:29 - 07:42] Speaker 2: So I think it's been interesting to see kind of as the technology's developed how, whether it's coaches or athletic trainers or strength and conditioning coaches have then taken the technology and said, hey, here's what I'm going to try and do with it.
[07:43 - 07:47] Speaker 2: What's been for me, that sometimes complicates the matter, right?
[07:47 - 07:51] Speaker 2: When folks are like, oh, this new tool, what's the metric that it provides?
[07:51 - 08:03] Speaker 2: And I think sometimes it's helpful to have the conversation to go back to the technology, whether it's brand new or one of the older pieces of technology, just to scale is a tool, right.
[08:03 - 08:10] Speaker 2: And it's not necessarily the tool itself, but how that tool gets used.
[08:11 - 08:17] Speaker 2: A great example that I had a conversation with a strength and conditioning coach in regards to a scale.
[08:17 - 08:24] Speaker 2: She had one team that they got on the scale at the beginning of practice and they got on the scale at the end of practice.
[08:25 - 08:30] Speaker 2: And the team culture, the climate, whether it's coaches or student athlete, nobody cared about the number.
[08:31 - 08:33] Speaker 2: It was all about, what's the difference?
[08:33 - 08:35] Speaker 2: So I know how much I need to drink.
[08:36 - 08:38] Speaker 2: There wasn't, oh, you weigh 152 today.
[08:38 - 08:39] Speaker 2: We need to have a conversation.
[08:40 - 08:43] Speaker 2: It was more, all right, you're at 152 now, you're at 148 after.
[08:44 - 08:45] Speaker 2: Here's how much you need to drink.
[08:46 - 08:56] Speaker 2: But she also talked about that she had another team that she wouldn't put a scale within 10 yards of the team because of complicating factors that it would have, whether it was body image or cultures.
[08:57 - 09:00] Speaker 2: And I think that, to me, helps simplify that.
[09:00 - 09:11] Speaker 2: These are really just tools that we have to really think about how they get implemented and how we're using them in each scenario and not say, oh, well, it works with this team, we need to use it with this team.
[09:12 - 09:14] Speaker 1: Yeah, that's a great point.
[09:14 - 09:20] Speaker 1: It reminds me of one quick thing before we use that as a perfect segue into my question for Mark.
[09:21 - 09:27] Speaker 1: But that is one of the biggest takeaways for me from the Performance Performance Tech Summit was that performance technologies are a tool.
[09:27 - 09:29] Speaker 1: They are not a solution.
[09:29 - 09:38] Speaker 1: And so it's really important for folks to remember that they can be very helpful in certain settings, but they aren't going to solve problems in and of themselves.
[09:38 - 09:39] Speaker 1: Right.
[09:39 - 09:46] Speaker 1: We still need to incorporate all the other parts around health, safety and performance to make sure we're really helping these student athletes succeed.
[09:47 - 09:54] Speaker 1: But it's a great transition into my question for you, Mark, where you sit on campus and your experience as an athletic trainer.
[09:54 - 10:00] Speaker 1: You see that at lot of athletic programs, they want to keep up with the latest technologies, right?
[10:00 - 10:03] Speaker 1: I saw that certainly at my time on campus.
[10:03 - 10:06] Speaker 1: And I know you both, you both see that now.
[10:06 - 10:15] Speaker 1: So, Mark, how can schools harness innovation but still prioritize student athlete health, safety and well being?
[10:16 - 10:17] Speaker 3: Yeah, that's a great question.
[10:17 - 10:30] Speaker 3: One we wrestle with often and one that interested me to participate in this group because of that, I think, you know, there's two lenses, there's performance lens and there's sports medicine lens, and it's still the same data.
[10:31 - 10:40] Speaker 3: And I think people are purchasing performance technologies a lot for fear of missing out that somebody else is doing something they're not.
[10:40 - 10:49] Speaker 3: When really the right approach to the performance technology should be how can we maximize our care or maximize our performance of our student athletes?
[10:49 - 11:02] Speaker 3: And what tools, as Tim alluded to, are available for us to be able to assess those particular areas and answer questions that we need to have answered, rather than just give us a bunch of data to collect on the athletes.
[11:02 - 11:12] Speaker 3: So, you know, how you can harness that is to actually go into the situation where you have questions you want answered about your student athletes.
[11:12 - 11:18] Speaker 3: And once you have the question, then you can find the technology that may or may not help guide you in that.
[11:18 - 11:24] Speaker 3: And I think one of the things I brought up and I've said a lot is we need to be data guided, not data driven.
[11:25 - 11:35] Speaker 3: And so it's Like Tim said, these are all just tools, and they're another marker or something to tell us, are we heading in a certain direction with a student athlete, or are we seeing a trend with a student athlete?
[11:36 - 11:41] Speaker 3: And that's from questionnaires to wearables to hardwired technology.
[11:41 - 11:42] Speaker 3: It's the same process.
[11:43 - 11:56] Speaker 3: So our technology to harness that should be selected for a specific purpose to help answer particular questions for the performance staff or the sports medicine staff, or both as they're doing that.
[11:56 - 12:05] Speaker 3: So that's the biggest thing that I think the sports medicine folks, we've always tried to use the best available tools.
[12:05 - 12:10] Speaker 3: Some of this technology answers questions for us that we had only subjective answers to in the past.
[12:11 - 12:18] Speaker 3: And so if we can find the tools to help guide us in those directions, it's very beneficial for the care and performance of student athlete.
[12:19 - 12:20] Speaker 1: Yeah, I think that makes a lot of sense.
[12:20 - 12:34] Speaker 1: When I think back to some of the performance technologies that I was using on campus or associated with the teams that were using it, It's a lot of data that you get from these technologies.
[12:34 - 12:42] Speaker 1: And I think, you know, admittedly, not everybody knew what to do with all of those data.
[12:42 - 12:50] Speaker 1: And so starting with the question, what is it that I would like to help student athletes with?
[12:50 - 12:51] Speaker 1: Is it speed?
[12:51 - 12:51] Speaker 1: Is it strength?
[12:51 - 12:53] Speaker 1: Is it explosivity?
[12:54 - 12:54] Speaker 1: Right.
[12:55 - 13:14] Speaker 1: And then trying to find the appropriate technology to answer that particular question, I think it makes sense from a financial standpoint, as campuses right now more than ever are battling with having to balance financial priorities across athletic budgets.
[13:15 - 13:19] Speaker 1: So I think it overall is great advice.
[13:20 - 13:35] Speaker 1: Mark, talk to us a little bit about the importance of a written plan for performance technologies and what might be some of the sample elements that schools should be thinking about as they think about a written plan.
[13:37 - 13:46] Speaker 3: Yeah, I think one of the things we looked into was and had to be aware of was the unintended consequences of the data.
[13:47 - 13:50] Speaker 3: When you're trying to write a policy on how do you want to incorporate this?
[13:50 - 14:03] Speaker 3: And that took a lot of education from our counterparts in professional sports and what they'd experienced, you know, between the leagues and the players associations and what they've gone through with data.
[14:04 - 14:13] Speaker 3: So if you're going to have a written plan on how to incorporate it, it should address the factors that might lead to some unintended consequences or misuse of data.
[14:14 - 14:19] Speaker 3: And so using that as a starting point, we started saying, okay, if we want to.
[14:20 - 14:26] Speaker 3: Somebody wants to purchase some technology, the first thing we ask is, what is it you're trying to answer?
[14:26 - 14:30] Speaker 3: And how can that Contribute to what we may or may not already have to do that?
[14:30 - 14:38] Speaker 3: So a global question for an example might be, is our team getting tired during the course of the season?
[14:38 - 14:45] Speaker 3: And there are a lot of technologies that will tell you, they can tell you that, but they're going to give you a little snapshot of that.
[14:45 - 14:51] Speaker 3: And so if, if that's the case, if that's a technology you want to help monitor that, what is that technology?
[14:53 - 14:54] Speaker 3: Has it been proven to be valid?
[14:54 - 14:58] Speaker 3: Has it proven to be reliable so we can trust the data?
[14:58 - 15:05] Speaker 3: And then how are we going to execute monitoring that and what actions are we going to take as a result of that?
[15:05 - 15:16] Speaker 3: Is it going to be incorporated into a larger picture of three technologies that might be telling us that, and is that going to paint a bigger picture for us of what's going on with the student athlete?
[15:16 - 15:18] Speaker 3: And ideally, that's what you want.
[15:18 - 15:19] Speaker 3: You want more data points.
[15:19 - 15:22] Speaker 3: Again, being data guided rather than data driven.
[15:23 - 15:42] Speaker 3: If you have four technologies that may give you some indication on athlete readiness or fatigue, and an athlete is showing deficient in three of those four, you probably better have a conversation with the athlete about what's going on versus being completely driven by one metric from one technology that tells you something might be going awry.
[15:42 - 15:56] Speaker 3: So with that in mind, you know, we started to put together policies and actually more procedures on if somebody wants to incorporate technology, they're going to have to answer the questions, has this, is it been shown to be valid?
[15:56 - 15:57] Speaker 3: Is it reliable?
[15:58 - 15:58] Speaker 3: Exactly.
[15:58 - 15:59] Speaker 3: How are we going to use it?
[16:00 - 16:02] Speaker 3: Who's going to have access to that data?
[16:03 - 16:04] Speaker 3: Who owns the data?
[16:04 - 16:07] Speaker 3: We get into that later, I think in another conversation later.
[16:07 - 16:08] Speaker 3: But how has that worked out?
[16:09 - 16:12] Speaker 3: And more importantly, what's the in the big picture?
[16:12 - 16:13] Speaker 3: How is this going to be incorporated?
[16:14 - 16:25] Speaker 3: And then once we have those questions, we actually have a form here we've developed for our people to fill that out so that we can actually look at that and say, does it fit into what we're trying to do here or not?
[16:25 - 16:29] Speaker 3: Or is it just something that somebody said, hey, another institution has this, we need it.
[16:29 - 16:33] Speaker 3: Well, we want to investigate that first and figure out how does it fit into everything we do here.
[16:33 - 16:43] Speaker 3: So I think we're certainly not perfect at it, but over the course of the last two or three years, that's what we've learned from a lot of our counterparts that have been doing this for maybe a little bit longer.
[16:44 - 16:46] Speaker 1: Yeah, those are excellent points.
[16:46 - 16:57] Speaker 1: Another thing that came to my mind when I was doing this on campus was this idea of how Often should we be reevaluating whether or not this technology is still helpful to us?
[16:57 - 16:58] Speaker 1: Right.
[16:58 - 16:59] Speaker 1: Because things change over time.
[16:59 - 17:03] Speaker 1: Teams change, needs change, financial situations change.
[17:03 - 17:14] Speaker 1: And so another part of that written plan may be, hey, going to reassess this and gather feedback from stakeholders and then make decisions about whether or not we continue.
[17:15 - 17:22] Speaker 1: So, Mark, I want to hear a little bit from you on this next question and then I'm going to kick it to Tim to get his take on it as well.
[17:22 - 17:24] Speaker 1: And it's about risks.
[17:24 - 17:34] Speaker 1: So you know, what risks could potentially arise if schools were to be using these technologies and not have written policies and procedures?
[17:35 - 17:39] Speaker 3: Yeah, I think that might kind of fall into two buckets.
[17:39 - 17:49] Speaker 3: There's always the chance of risk that if you're collecting data that could tell you that an athlete was really at risk for something and nobody paid attention to it and something happened that would put you at risk.
[17:49 - 17:52] Speaker 3: So that's one bucket.
[17:52 - 17:58] Speaker 3: The other risk that you might have is unintended consequences on the use of the data.
[17:58 - 17:58] Speaker 1: You.
[17:58 - 18:07] Speaker 3: And that a lot of times comes down to who has access to the data, who's interpreting the data, and what actions are being taken because of that data.
[18:07 - 18:12] Speaker 3: And so I think your policies should probably be written to address that.
[18:12 - 18:14] Speaker 3: I would go to follow up on your last point.
[18:14 - 18:26] Speaker 3: You know, reevaluating that technology that needs to be reevaluated, you know, quite often actually, and really the question needs to be asked is what actions have been taken because of this data?
[18:26 - 18:27] Speaker 3: Is it actionable?
[18:27 - 18:38] Speaker 3: And also, has there been anything that's gone on with this data that might be detrimental to the student athlete, to their mental well being, to the institution, to any other place?
[18:38 - 18:39] Speaker 3: And so there's a.
[18:39 - 18:47] Speaker 3: Because technology rapidly evolves and you're still learning about it, that has to be asked quite often and have a real honest conversation about that.
[18:47 - 18:56] Speaker 3: But the risk is protection of data, not acting on important data or misinterpreting the data and using it incorrectly.
[18:56 - 18:57] Speaker 3: So there is some risk involved.
[18:57 - 19:03] Speaker 3: Which again goes back to, you should have some policies on exactly why you're using the data and who's going to have access, et cetera.
[19:05 - 19:09] Speaker 2: And I'll add to Mark hits the nails on the head in regards to that risk piece.
[19:09 - 19:17] Speaker 2: The other piece that's been shown are some of the mental health pieces that fall in with the collection of some of this data.
[19:18 - 19:27] Speaker 2: There was a great study that looked at professional rugby players and they termed it data valence, like sort of like a data surveillance.
[19:27 - 19:40] Speaker 2: And these professional rugby players reported these aspects of Fear and anxiety, because the team was collecting and created their own metric, this work index rating.
[19:41 - 19:47] Speaker 2: And players were graded on what their work index was, but they had no clue what went into it.
[19:47 - 19:57] Speaker 2: They were expected to access a tablet with information that was collected on a regular basis and then graded if they didn't access it.
[19:58 - 20:04] Speaker 2: And so these players really talked about a lot of the anxiety and mental health issues that came out as part of that.
[20:04 - 20:15] Speaker 2: And I think we kind of see part of that too, when we talk about an education piece that sometimes the individuals who were collecting the data don't actually know what the data means.
[20:16 - 20:32] Speaker 2: If you're going to grade someone and say, hey, you need to have them be at a certain percentage of your heart rate to show that you're actually exhibiting effort is not actually an accurate use of heart rate data, but we've seen that there are concerns with it.
[20:32 - 20:49] Speaker 2: Another group looked at individuals using accelerometers, and while I think it was like 80% of the users had used some sort of GPS or accelerometer, an overwhelming majority of them couldn't define what acceleration was accurately.
[20:50 - 20:59] Speaker 2: And I think that gives some, really some pause to being able to interpret the data and use it accurately if folks can't accurately define them.
[21:00 - 21:05] Speaker 1: Yeah, that's a great segue into my next question, which was going to be about education.
[21:05 - 21:21] Speaker 1: I remember we spoke for a long time about this during the summit, this concept of making sure that every stakeholder involved in this process is educated about the use of this technology.
[21:22 - 21:32] Speaker 1: So I'll open this up to either of you, but who specifically should be receiving education about performance technology and why specifically should they be?
[21:34 - 21:36] Speaker 3: I can kind of lead that one off.
[21:36 - 21:46] Speaker 3: I think, obviously, you know, your performance staff, your strength and conditioning coaches, and people associated with that need education on all the above.
[21:46 - 21:48] Speaker 3: What is each piece of technology?
[21:49 - 21:51] Speaker 3: How valid and reliable is it?
[21:51 - 21:55] Speaker 3: How are we intending to use this and who's interpreting it?
[21:56 - 21:57] Speaker 3: Tim's right.
[21:57 - 22:05] Speaker 3: You know, I think a lot of people are given technology and it's marketed that here's the number you need to know or need to hit, need to see.
[22:05 - 22:07] Speaker 3: And none of that's really been validated.
[22:08 - 22:10] Speaker 3: Data is individual per athlete.
[22:10 - 22:24] Speaker 3: And so there needs to be a real strong, strong education component of the performance staff and the sports medicine staff on exactly what this data is and what it means and how it's going to be utilized in an agreement across all parties.
[22:25 - 22:28] Speaker 3: On, yes, we agree this is how we're going to approach this and do that.
[22:28 - 22:43] Speaker 3: I think there obviously needs to be Education with the coaching staff, maybe not quite as deep, but if we're going to use technologies that may impact what they're going to do, exactly what that technology is, how it works, how we think we're going to utilize it and help.
[22:43 - 22:48] Speaker 3: Help guide our decisions, kind of, you know, and so.
[22:48 - 22:51] Speaker 3: And then lastly, the most important piece is probably the student athlete.
[22:51 - 23:04] Speaker 3: So if you're going to have them where technology or they're going to utilize technology, there needs to be some education on, hey, this is what we're using, here's how we're using it, here's what it's used for, here's who's going to have access to that data.
[23:05 - 23:11] Speaker 3: And athletes should have the right, like Tim said earlier, they should have the right to not participate with data if they don't want to.
[23:12 - 23:13] Speaker 3: You know.
[23:13 - 23:16] Speaker 3: And so some data they can choose, some data is out of their control.
[23:16 - 23:23] Speaker 3: If somebody's using a TV monitoring system that's going to measure court speeds, you can't really control that because that's already being done.
[23:23 - 23:29] Speaker 3: But certainly a wearable or doing some other kind of device with an athlete would require their consent.
[23:29 - 23:33] Speaker 3: And so that's one of the things that probably most people are not doing.
[23:34 - 23:37] Speaker 3: And obviously it's one thing, I know we have to get better at that as well.
[23:37 - 23:44] Speaker 3: But educating the athletes and making sure we have consent from them that we're going to use it, and they know exactly the parameters of everything that's going on.
[23:46 - 23:58] Speaker 1: And this stuff is hard, right, because these companies come in selling you their technology and they're confident in the way they talk about what this technology is going to be able to bring to your team.
[23:58 - 24:12] Speaker 1: And that's why I think it's really important for campuses to understand that you've got to do your own homework and you've got to look into the stuff, the reliability and the validity of some of these technologies to figure out if it really is the right one for you.
[24:13 - 24:15] Speaker 1: And back to your comments about the student athletes.
[24:15 - 24:17] Speaker 1: Mark, I couldn't agree more.
[24:17 - 24:23] Speaker 1: And I remember the student athletes that were participating in the summit and some of the comments that they shared with us about their experiences.
[24:24 - 24:28] Speaker 1: And I remember drawing on my own experience with performance tech.
[24:29 - 24:46] Speaker 1: Sometimes the inadvertent harms that come with these technologies for student athletes would outweigh any potential benefit that you might think you're getting from it, which is why having the conversation with the student athlete is important to understand, what is this data?
[24:46 - 24:49] Speaker 1: What effect is this data having on you?
[24:49 - 24:50] Speaker 1: Is it helping you?
[24:50 - 24:52] Speaker 1: Do you Feel like it's helping you.
[24:52 - 24:59] Speaker 1: Those are really important questions to ask, and I think the education part of the recommendations reinforces that.
[25:00 - 25:09] Speaker 1: Before we leave this topic, I do want to see if either of you have anything to add in terms of the misconceptions that are out there about performance tech.
[25:09 - 25:14] Speaker 1: I mean, I know we've talked a little bit about, are they really doing what they say they're doing?
[25:14 - 25:21] Speaker 1: Are there any other misconceptions as it pertains to the data or the technologies themselves that you care to discuss?
[25:23 - 25:32] Speaker 2: I think for me that the challenge that a lot of athletic staff has is a lot of these performance tech companies have their big claims.

[29:10 - 29:10] Speaker 1: Excellent.

[29:57 - 29:57] Speaker 1: Right.

[30:01 - 30:02] Speaker 1: How are folks storing it?

[30:13 - 30:20] Speaker 2: So as I started looking into some of this data, I initially thought, oh, well, we're collecting health data, so it's got to be protected by hipaa.

[30:35 - 30:39] Speaker 2: The biggest recommendation that I would make to folks is talk with your general counsel.

[30:50 - 31:06] Speaker 2: And I think individuals on campuses, based on the conversations I've had, don't necessarily oftentimes see this type of data as either health data or as performance that needs to be protected.

[31:14 - 31:23] Speaker 2: Instead of understanding that these can be really personable, they can be really intimate data and be identifiable for individuals.

[42:10 - 42:14] Speaker 3: Value driven for us is really return on investment.
[42:15 - 42:22] Speaker 3: In other words, did we, whatever we invested in, did it help us accomplish what we were trying to accomplish?
[42:23 - 42:26] Speaker 3: And I don't think we do that nearly enough.
[42:26 - 42:30] Speaker 3: I think we adopt something and then we just keep it and we keep utilizing it.
[42:30 - 42:31] Speaker 3: I think Tim was right.
[42:31 - 42:42] Speaker 3: You've got to go back and do a regular evaluation on, hey, is this technology really giving us the information that we desired and is it helping us make decisions?
[42:42 - 42:45] Speaker 3: Again, if we're not acting on the data, we shouldn't be collecting it.
[42:45 - 42:50] Speaker 3: And so I think for us that's really what value driven means.

[42:59 - 43:00] Speaker 3: How is it impacting our decisions?

[43:22 - 43:24] Speaker 3: And then at the end of the day, did it help you answer those?
[43:24 - 43:28] Speaker 3: Was the value shown in the investment that you made in that technology?
